concept.name: Mutual TLS Between Services

relationships.description: Connects Mutual TLS Between Services to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Mutual TLS (mTLS) extends standard TLS so both the client and server present and cryptographically verify X.509 certificates during the handshake. In microservice and zero-trust architectures, mTLS replaces fragile static API keys and IP allowlists with automated, short-lived cryptographic workload identities.
spark.keyTakeaway: Standard TLS proves who the server is; mTLS proves who both sides are on every connection, enabling zero-trust service-to-service authentication and encryption in transit.

concept.whyItMatters: Perimeter firewalls and VPC IP allowlists collapse the moment an attacker compromises a single pod or moves laterally inside a cluster. Static bearer tokens or shared API keys leak in logs and rarely rotate. mTLS binds a cryptographic identity (such as a SPIFFE URI SAN) directly to each workload, encrypting all east-west traffic via TLS 1.3 and enforcing fine-grained authorization at the L4/L7 proxy.
whenToUse: Service-to-service (east-west) traffic in Kubernetes, multi-cloud, or hybrid networks handling sensitive PII, financial, or regulated workloads (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMP).
B2B partner APIs and webhook callbacks (e.g., Open Banking, payment gateways) where strong cryptographic client identity is required beyond a shared secret.
Zero-trust environments where network location (same VPC/subnet) must not grant implicit trust.
whenNotToUse: Public consumer browsers or mobile apps—managing client certificates across millions of end-user devices is operationally brutal compared to OAuth2/OIDC + Passkeys.
Ultra-low-latency, single-host IPC or tightly coupled processes where TLS handshake/encryption overhead breaks sub-100-microsecond budgets and host isolation suffices.
Teams without automated certificate issuance and rotation (e.g., SPIRE, cert-manager, Vault PKI)—manual mTLS cert management guarantees self-inflicted outages.
keyPoints: Authentication is bidirectional: in TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446), the server sends `CertificateRequest`, and the client replies with its `Certificate` and `CertificateVerify` signature.
Use short-lived certificates (e.g., 1–24 hour TTL) rotated automatically in memory—short TTLs eliminate the need for fragile CRL/OCSP revocation checks inside the cluster.

Authorize on **identity, not just trust**: verifying a cert is signed by your CA only proves the caller is in your org; always check the SAN (`spiffe://prod.mesh/ns/payments/sa/checkout`) against an allowlist.
Offload mTLS to a sidecar or ambient proxy (Envoy/Istio, Linkerd) so application code stays clean, or use native libraries when zero-hop memory isolation is required.
Connection pooling (HTTP/2 / gRPC keep-alive) amortizes the 1-RTT TLS 1.3 handshake cost down to near-zero on steady-state traffic.

examples.title: Kubernetes Zero-Trust Mesh with Istio + SPIFFE
examples.scenario: A healthcare platform runs 60 microservices on EKS. Istio's `istiod` acts as the RA/CA, minting 24-hour X.509 SVIDs (`spiffe://cluster.local/ns/billing/sa/invoice`) to Envoy sidecars and enforcing `PeerAuthentication: STRICT`.
examples.outcome: All pod-to-pod traffic is encrypted and authenticated automatically; an AuthorizationPolicy blocks the analytics service from calling the patient-records API even on the same node.

examples.title: Open Banking Partner API Gateway
examples.scenario: A bank's API gateway requires fintech partners to present EV/OV client certificates signed by a trusted Open Banking CA alongside OAuth2 DPoP/client credentials.
examples.outcome: Even if a partner's OAuth client secret leaks, an attacker cannot replay tokens without possessing the partner's HSM-backed mTLS private key.

tradeOffs.pro: Sidecars centralize cert rotation, cipher suites, and authz policies across polyglot services (Java, Python, Go) with zero app code changes.
tradeOffs.con: Adds ~1–3ms P99 latency per hop and 50–150MB RAM overhead per pod.

tradeOffs.pro: 24-hour certs limit blast radius on key compromise and remove OCSP/CRL lookup dependencies.
tradeOffs.con: Requires rock-solid automated rotation (SPIRE/cert-manager) and tight NTP clock sync across all nodes.

tradeOffs.pro: Permissive mode accepts both plaintext and mTLS during migration, preventing instant outages.
tradeOffs.con: Leaving services in Permissive mode indefinitely creates a silent downgrade hole.

failureModes.name: Expired Root or Intermediate CA
failureModes.description: Leaf certs rotate fine, but an unmonitored intermediate CA expires at 02:00 UTC, causing 100% of service-to-service TLS handshakes to fail simultaneously.
failureModes.mitigation: Alert on CA expiration at 90/30/7 days, automate intermediate CA rotation with overlapping trust bundles (2-CA overlap), and test rotation in staging.

failureModes.name: Missing SAN Authorization (AuthN != AuthZ)
failureModes.description: A service validates that the client cert was signed by the corporate CA, but never checks *which* service's cert it is—allowing a compromised dev/metrics pod to call the admin payment API.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce explicit L7 AuthorizationPolicies matching exact SPIFFE URIs or CN/SAN patterns per route.

failureModes.name: Clock Skew Rejecting Fresh Certs
failureModes.description: A newly provisioned VM's clock lags by 5 minutes; when it receives a newly minted cert (`NotBefore = now`), peers reject it as 'not yet valid'.
failureModes.mitigation: Backdate `NotBefore` by 2–5 minutes during cert issuance (standard in SPIRE/Vault) and monitor NTP drift.

failureModes.name: Handshake Storm on Pod Churn
failureModes.description: Hundreds of pods restart simultaneously without session resumption or HTTP/2 pooling, saturating CPU with asymmetric ECDHE/RSA handshakes.
failureModes.mitigation: Use ECDSA P-256 keys (much faster signing than RSA-2048), enable TLS 1.3 session tickets, and configure long-lived HTTP/2/gRPC connection pools.

commonMistakes: Hand-rolling OpenSSL scripts and cron jobs to distribute `.pem` files instead of using SPIRE, cert-manager, or HashiCorp Vault PKI.
Logging or passing raw unvalidated `X-Forwarded-Client-Cert` (XFCC) headers from untrusted hops—always strip XFCC at the edge ingress.
Assuming mTLS alone authorizes every action; mTLS authenticates the *calling service*, not the end-user (pair mTLS with JWTs for end-user context).
Using `InsecureSkipVerify: true` in staging and accidentally shipping it to production.
Forgetting health-check probes: Kubernetes `kubelet` HTTP probes don't have mesh client certs unless the proxy/app exempts `/healthz` or uses `PERMISSIVE` on the probe port.

sections.content:
## The idea

In standard TLS (HTTPS), only the server presents a certificate; the client stays anonymous at the transport layer and must authenticate later via cookies, API keys, or bearer tokens. **Mutual TLS (mTLS)** makes certificate verification **bidirectional**: during the TLS 1.3 handshake, the server sends a `CertificateRequest`, and the client must present a valid X.509 certificate and prove possession of its private key via `CertificateVerify`.

In modern distributed systems, mTLS is the cryptographic foundation of **Zero Trust** networking. Instead of trusting a packet because it originated from `10.42.x.x`, every workload carries a short-lived cryptographic identity (like a SPIFFE ID) minted by an automated CA and verified on every connection.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace `checkout-svc` calling `payment-svc` over an Istio/Envoy mTLS mesh:

1. **Identity Issuance**: On startup (and every 12 hours), `checkout-svc`'s Envoy sidecar sends a CSR via Unix domain socket (SDS) to `istiod`/SPIRE, proving its Kubernetes ServiceAccount JWT. It receives an ECDSA P-256 X.509 SVID with SAN `spiffe://prod.mesh/ns/orders/sa/checkout`.
2. **TLS 1.3 Handshake**: `checkout-svc` opens a TCP connection to `payment-svc`'s sidecar. In 1 RTT, `payment-svc` sends its certificate + `CertificateRequest`; `checkout-svc` responds with its own certificate and `CertificateVerify` signature.
3. **Trust & SAN Verification**: Both Envoy proxies validate certificate chains against the shared root CA trust bundle.
4. **Policy Enforcement**: `payment-svc`'s Envoy evaluates its `AuthorizationPolicy`: only `spiffe://prod.mesh/ns/orders/sa/checkout` is allowed to `POST /v1/charge`.
5. **Encrypted Reuse**: The authenticated TLS 1.3 channel stays open as an HTTP/2 / gRPC multiplexed pool, serving thousands of RPCs with zero extra handshake cost.

sections.content:
## Certificate lifecycle and CA rotation

The hardest part of mTLS is not the handshake—it is **zero-downtime rotation**. Leaf certificates should be short-lived (1–24 hours) and rotated at 50% of their lifetime via in-memory APIs (Envoy SDS or SPIFFE Workload API), never written to persistent disks where they can leak.

Root and intermediate CA rotation requires a **two-step trust-bundle overlap**: first distribute both `Old_CA` and `New_CA` in every workload's trust bundle; once 100% of pods trust both, switch the issuer to mint leaf certs under `New_CA`; finally, after all old leaf TTLs expire, prune `Old_CA`.

## mTLS implementation approaches

| Approach | App Code Changes | Language Support | Rotation Automation | Latency Overhead | Best Fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Sidecar Mesh** (Istio / Linkerd) | None | Polyglot (any language) | Built-in (SDS / SPIFFE) | ~1–3ms per hop | Kubernetes microservice fleets |
| **Ambient / eBPF Mesh** (Istio Ambient / Cilium) | None | Polyglot (node-level) | Built-in | <1ms (shared ztunnel) | High-density clusters reducing sidecar RAM |
| **In-App SDK** (go-spiffe / Java SSLContext) | Moderate | Per-language library | Requires SPIRE agent or Vault | <0.3ms (no extra hop) | Ultra-low-latency or non-mesh VMs |
| **Edge API Gateway** (Envoy / NGINX / Cloudflare) | Minimal (read headers) | Polyglot behind gateway | Vault / cert-manager / ACM | ~1ms at ingress | B2B partner APIs & external webhooks |

## Failure modes

The classic mTLS catastrophe is **silent CA expiration**: leaf certs rotate every 24 hours so everything looks healthy until the 1-year intermediate CA expires and drops 100% of cluster traffic simultaneously. Always monitor CA `NotAfter` timestamps independently from leaf certs.

Another common trap is **confusing authentication with authorization**: if every pod in your cluster shares the same root CA and your server only validates the CA signature without inspecting the SAN, a compromised logging sidecar can impersonate the billing service.

## Zero-downtime migration playbook

Never flip an existing production cluster straight to `STRICT` mTLS. Roll out in three phases:

1. **Permissive + Telemetry**: Deploy sidecars or TLS listeners in `PERMISSIVE` mode (accepting both plaintext and mTLS) and verify via Prometheus metrics (`istio_requests_total{connection_security_policy="mutual_tls"}`) that clients are upgrading.
2. **Fix Exceptions**: Exempt or adapt Kubernetes `kubelet` probes, legacy cron jobs, and external ingress gateways.
3. **Enforce Strict + AuthZ**: Flip namespace by namespace to `STRICT`, then layer L7 `AuthorizationPolicy` rules matching exact SANs.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] **Automate issuance**: Use SPIRE, `istiod`, `cert-manager`, or Vault PKI—never manage `.pem` files manually.
- [ ] **Enforce TLS 1.3 + ECDSA P-256**: Cut handshake latency and CPU cost while eliminating legacy TLS 1.0/1.1 ciphers.
- [ ] **Authorize on SANs**: Validate exact SPIFFE URI or SAN allowlists on sensitive routes, not just CA trust.
- [ ] **Handle clock skew**: Backdate `NotBefore` by 2–5 minutes and alert on NTP drift.
- [ ] **Monitor CA expiry**: Alert at 90, 30, and 7 days before intermediate/root CA expiration and rehearse 2-CA overlap rotation.
- [ ] **Strip untrusted headers**: Sanitize `X-Forwarded-Client-Cert` at the edge so external callers cannot spoof internal identities.

interviewProblems.title: Mutual TLS Between Services
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Mutual TLS Between Services. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Mutual TLS (mTLS) extends standard TLS so both the client and server present and cryptographically verify X.509 certificates during the handshake. In microservice and zero-trust architectures, mTLS replaces fragile static API keys and IP allowlists with automated, short-lived cryptographic workload identities.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Server Sidecar applies the primary invariant and coordinates with AuthZ Policy Engine.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, AuthZ Policy Engine experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Alert on CA expiration at 90/30/7 days, automate intermediate CA rotation with overlapping trust bundles (2-CA overlap), and test rotation in staging.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Standard TLS proves who the server is; mTLS proves who both sides are on every connection, enabling zero-trust service-to-service authentication and encryption in transit.
Avoid trap: Hand-rolling OpenSSL scripts and cron jobs to distribute `.pem` files instead of using SPIRE, cert-manager, or HashiCorp Vault PKI.
Avoid trap: Logging or passing raw unvalidated `X-Forwarded-Client-Cert` (XFCC) headers from untrusted hops—always strip XFCC at the edge ingress.
When to reach for it: Service-to-service (east-west) traffic in Kubernetes, multi-cloud, or hybrid networks handling sensitive PII, financial, or regulated workloads (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMP).
When to reach for it: B2B partner APIs and webhook callbacks (e.g., Open Banking, payment gateways) where strong cryptographic client identity is required beyond a shared secret.

putItTogether.title: Putting Mutual Tls Services Together
putItTogether.summary: Standard TLS proves who the server is; mTLS proves who both sides are on every connection, enabling zero-trust service-to-service authentication and encryption in transit.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Mutual Tls Services before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: All pod-to-pod traffic is encrypted and authenticated automatically; an AuthorizationPolicy blocks the analytics service from calling the patient-records API even on the same node.
